quote: "And let them know that in worshipping the Lord in the flesh we do not worship a creature, but, as we said above, the Creator Who has put on the created body." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 60, Section 6
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 60, Section 6

quote: "For He has become Man, that He might deify us in Himself, and He has been born of a woman, and begotten of a Virgin, in order to transfer to Himself our erring generation, and that we may become henceforth a holy race, and 'partakers of the Divine Nature [2 Peter 1:4],' as blessed Peter wrote." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 60, Section 4
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 60, Section 4

quote: "If the Word were a creature, He would not assume the created body to quicken it. For what help can creatures derive from a creature that itself needs salvation?" -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 60, Section 8
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 60, Section 8

quote: "For the Flesh did not diminish the glory of the Word; far be the thought: on the contrary, it was glorified by Him. Nor, because the Son that was in the form of God took upon Him the form of a servant [Philippians 2:6-7] was He deprived of His Godhead. On the contrary, He is thus become the Deliverer of all flesh and of all creation." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 60, Section 4
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 60, Section 4

quote: "He put on the creature, that He as creator might once more consecrate it, and be able to recover it." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 60, Section 8
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 60, Section 8

quote: "And we neither divide the body, being such, from the Word, and worship it by itself, nor when we wish to worship the Word do we set Him far apart from the Flesh, but knowing, as we said above, that 'the Word was made flesh [John 1:14],' we recognise Him as God also, after having come in the flesh. Who, accordingly, is so senseless as to say to the Lord: 'Leave the Body that I may worship Thee;' or so impious as to join the senseless Jews in saying, on account of the Body, 'Why dost Thou, being a man, make Thyself God [John 10:33]?'" -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 60, Section 3
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 60, Section 3

quote: "We do not worship a creature. Far be the thought. For such an error belongs to heathens and Arians. But we worship the Lord of Creation, Incarnate, the Word of God." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 60, Section 3
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 60, Section 3

quote: "[i.e., Bishop Alexander praying to God:] 'If Arius is brought to communion to-morrow, let me Thy servant depart, and destroy not the pious with the impious; but if Thou wilt spare Thy Church (and I know that Thou wilt spare), look upon the words of Eusebius and his fellows, and give not thine inheritance to destruction and reproach, and take off Arius, lest if he enter into the Church, the heresy also may seem to enter with him, and henceforward impiety be accounted for piety.' When the Bishop had thus prayed...a wonderful and extraordinary circumstance took place...Arius...urged by the necessities of nature withdrew, and suddenly, in the language of Scripture, 'falling headlong he burst asunder in the midst [Acts 1:18],' and immediately expired as he lay, and was deprived both of communion [i.e., to the Church] and of his life together." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 54, Section 3
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 54, Section 3

quote: "Arius had been invited by the Emperor Constantine, through the interest of Eusebius and his fellows; and when he entered the presence the Emperor enquired of him, whether he held the Faith of the Catholic Church? And he declared upon oath that he held the right Faith, and gave in an account of his Faith in writing, suppressing the points for which he had been cast out of the Church by the Bishop Alexander, and speciously alleging expressions out of the Scriptures. When therefore he swore that he did not profess the opinions for which Alexander had excommunicated him, [the Emperor] dismissed him, saying, 'If thy Faith be right, thou hast done well to swear; but if thy Faith be impious, and thou hast sworn, God judge of thee according to thy oath'." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 54, Section 2
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 54, Section 2

quote: "And we are specially bound to fly from the communion of men whose opinions we hold in execration [i.e., cursed, anathema, denouncement, etc.]...But if any pretend that he confesses the right faith, but appear to communicate with those others, exhort him to abstain from such communion, and if he promise to do so, treat him as a brother, but if he persist in a contentious spirit, him avoid." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 53
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 53

quote: "For although it be impossible to comprehend what God is, yet it is possible to say what He is not." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 52, Section 2
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 52, Section 2

quote: "Accordingly we...desire to hold the Apostolic tradition, and to live according to the commands of the divine law." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 51
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 51

quote: "So the antichristian gang of the Arian madmen has been shewn [i.e., through the embarrassing and gruesome death of Arius spoken of in Section 3] to be unpleasing to God and impious; and many of those who before were deceived by it changed their opinions." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 54, Section 4
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 54, Section 4

quote: "And will not he who takes up the support of that which He has made excommunicate [i.e., believing condemned heresy], be guilty of great impiety, and manifestly an enemy of Christ?" -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 54, Section 4
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 54, Section 4

quote: "Such has been the end of Arius [i.e., the events detailed in Section 3]: and Eusebius and his fellows, overwhelmed with shame, buried their accomplice, while the blessed Alexander, amidst the rejoicings of the Church, celebrated the Communion with piety and orthodoxy, praying with all the brethren, and greatly glorifying God, not as exulting in his death (God forbid!), for 'it is appointed unto all men once to die [Hebrews 9:27],' but because this thing had been shewn forth in a manner transcending human judgments." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 54, Section 4
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 54, Section 4
tags: how to know the true Church

quote: "Let then those that repent openly anathematize by name the error of Eudoxius and Euzoius. For they blasphemed still, and wrote that He was a creature, ringleaders of the Arian heresy. But let them confess the faith confessed by the fathers at Nicaea, and that they put no other synod before that one." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 55
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 55

quote: "Certain heretics presumed to tamper with it [i.e., the true faith]. For a certain Arius and those with him attempted to corrupt it, and to introduce impiety in its place, affirming that the Son of God was from nought, and a creature, and a thing made and changeable." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 56, Section 1
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 56, Section 1

quote: "But since now certain who wish to renew the Arian heresy have presumed to set at nought this faith confessed at Nicaea by the Fathers, and while pretending to confess it, do in fact deny it...and blaspheming of their own accord against the Holy Spirit, in affirming that It is a creature, and came into being as a thing made by the Son." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 56, Section 1
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 56, Section 1

quote: "For one must not grieve over one that is gone to the place where grief is not." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 58
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 58

quote: "For whom do Arians spare, who have spared not even their own souls? Or how can they give up their infamous actions while they persist in denying Christ our Lord the only Son of God? This is the root of their wickedness; on this foundation of sand they build up the perversity of their ways, as we find it written in the thirteenth Psalm, 'The fool said in his heart there is no God [Psalm 13(14):1];' and presently follows, 'Corrupt are they and become abominable in their works.' Hence the Jews who denied the Son of God, deserved to be called 'a sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, a seed of evil doers, children without law [Isaiah 1:4].' Why 'without law?'—because you have deserted the Lord." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 51
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 51
tags: exclusion from the kingdom of Heaven

quote: "But let a man, wherever he is, strive earnestly; for the crown is given not according to position, but according to action." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 49, Section 9
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 49, Section 9

quote: "For you [i.e., Dracontius, whom Saint Athanasius is writing this letter to] are not the only one who has been elected from among monks, nor the only one to have presided over a monastery, or to have been beloved by monks." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 49, Section 7
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 49, Section 7

quote: "For we ought to walk by the standard of the saints and the fathers, and imitate them, and to be sure that if we depart from them we put ourselves also out of their fellowship." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 49, Section 4
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 49, Section 4

quote: "For the Faith there confessed by the Fathers [i.e., at the First Council of Nicaea] according to the divine Scriptures is enough by itself at once to overthrow all impiety, and to establish the religious belief in Christ." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 1
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 1

quote: "For the statements [i.e., those from Section 2: Christ is not divine, Christ's human body is eternal, etc.] are not fit for Christians to make or to hear, on the contrary they are in every way alien from the Apostolic teaching." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 3
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 3

quote: "While in saying that He has been changed into flesh, you imagine a change of the Word Himself. And who will tolerate you any longer if you so much as utter these opinions? For you have gone further in impiety than any heresy. For if the Word is coessential with the Body, the commemoration and the work of Mary are superfluous, inasmuch as the body could have existed before Mary, just as the Word also is eternal: if, that is, it is as you say co-essential with the Body. Or what need was there even of the Word coming among us, to put on what was coessential with Himself, or to change His own nature and become a body? For the Deity does not take hold of itself, so as to put on what is of its own Essence, any more than the Word sinned, in that it ransoms the sins of others, in order that changing into a body it should offer itself a sacrifice for itself, and ransom itself." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 4
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 4

quote: "For if all were of the same mind as your present advisers [i.e., the people who were telling Dracontius not to accept the office of bishop], how would you have become a Christian, since there would be no bishops? Or if our successors are to inherit this state of mind, how will the Churches be able to hold together?" -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 49, Section 4
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 49, Section 4

quote: "'Quicken me according to Thy Word [Psalm 118(119):107];' but by 'Thy Word,' is meant that we should serve Him with a pure heart." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 48
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 48

quote: "It is not right to kill, yet in war it is lawful and praiseworthy to destroy the enemy...the same act is at one time and under some circumstances unlawful, while under others, and at the right time, it is lawful and permissible." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 48
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 48

quote: "I marvel also at the craft of the devil, in that, although he is corruption and mischief itself, he suggests thoughts under the show of purity; but with the result of a snare rather than a test. For with the object, as I said before, of distracting ascetics from their customary and salutary meditation, and of appearing to overcome them, he stirs some such buzzing thoughts as are of no profit in life, vain questions and frivolities which one ought to put aside." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 48
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 48

quote: "But since the devil’s darts are varied and subtle, and he contrives to trouble those who are of simpler mind, and tries to hinder the ordinary exercises of the brethren, scattering secretly among them thoughts of uncleanness and defilement." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 48
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 48

quote: "On account of these deeds then [i.e., the persecution from the Arians], and all the others which they have committed against the Churches, the holy general council has deposed them all [i.e., Eusebius, Theodore, Narcissus, Valens, Ursacius, George, Stephen, Acacius, Menophantus, and their colleagues], and not only has judged them aliens from the Church, but has held them unworthy to be called Christians. For how can men be called Christians who deny Christ? And how can men be admitted to church who do evil against the Churches?" -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 47
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 47

quote: "He Himself [i.e., the Word] went to preach [i.e., to the dead in Hades], while the Body Joseph wrapped in a linen cloth, and laid it away at Golgotha. And so it is shewn to all that the Body was not the Word, but Body of the Word." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 6
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 6

quote: "And verily it is strange that He it was Who suffered and yet suffered not. Suffered, because His own Body suffered, and He was in it, which thus suffered; suffered not, because the Word, being by Nature God, is impassible." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 6
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 6

quote: "But this He did [i.e., take on a human body], and so it was, in order that Himself taking what was ours and offering it as a sacrifice, He might do away with it, and conversely might invest us with what was His [i.e., divinity], and cause the Apostle to say: 'This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal put on immortality [1 Corinthians 15:53]'." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 6
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 6

quote: "For if the Word were in the Body putatively, as they say, and by putative is meant imaginary, it follows that both the salvation and the resurrection of man is apparent only, as the most impious Manichaeus held. But truly our salvation is not merely apparent, nor does it extend to the body only, but the whole man, body and soul alike, has truly obtained salvation in the Word Himself." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 7
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 7

quote: "Whence they can be refuted who have ventured to say that the Lord was transformed into flesh and bones. For He did not say, 'As ye see Me to be flesh and bone,' but 'as ye see Me to have [Luke 24:39],' in order that it might not be thought that the Word Himself was changed into these things, but that He might be believed to have them after His resurrection as well as before His death." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 7
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 7

quote: "For what John said, 'The Word was made flesh [John 1:14],' has this meaning [i.e., that the Divine Person of the Word took on human nature and was not transformed into flesh and bones], as we may see by a similar passage; for it is written in Paul: 'Christ has become a curse for us [Galatians 3:13].' And just as He has not Himself become a curse, but is said to have done so because He took upon Him the curse on our behalf, so also He has become flesh not by being changed into flesh, but because He assumed on our behalf living flesh, and has become Man." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 8
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 8

quote: "For if (they argue) we say the Body is of one Essence with the Word, the Triad remains a Triad; for then the Word imports no foreign element into it; but if we admit that the Body derived from Mary is human, it follows, since the Body is foreign in Essence, and the Word is in it, that the addition of the Body causes a Tetrad instead of a Triad." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 8
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 8

quote: "Or who devised this abominable impiety, for it to enter even his imagination, and for him to say that to pronounce the Lord’s Body to be of Mary is to hold a Tetrad instead of a Triad in the Godhead? Those who think thus, saying that the Body of the Savior which He put on from Mary, is of the Essence of the Triad. Or whence again have certain vomited an impiety as great as those already mentioned; saying namely, that the body is not newer than the Godhead of the Word, but was coeternal with it always, since it was compounded of the Essence of Wisdom." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 2
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 2

quote: "And how do these remain Christians who imagine another God in addition to the true one?...For...they go very far wrong, so much so as to make the creature equal to the Creator, and suppose that the Godhead can receive an addition [i.e., speaking of those who say Christ's Body was coeternal/coessential in the Godhead: a form of Apollinarianism]." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 9
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 9

quote: "In the Triad one Godhead is recognized, and so in the Church one God is preached, the Father of the Word." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 9
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 9

quote: "For if He were not God in the Body, how came He, upon proceeding from Mary, straightway to be called 'Emmanuel, which is being interpreted God with us [Matthew 1:23]?' Why again...did Paul write...'of whom is Christ after the flesh, Who is above all God blessed for ever. Amen [Romans 9:5]'." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 10
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 10

quote: "For you yourselves, beloved, are not ignorant what the successors of the ill-named heresy of Eusebius did, namely Theodore, Narcissus, Valens, Ursacius, and the worst of them all, George, Stephen, Acacius, Menophantus, and their colleagues, for their madness is manifest to all; nor has it escaped your observation what they committed against the Churches." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 47
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 47

quote: "What lower region has vomited the statement that the Body born of Mary is coessential with the Godhead of the Word? or that the Word has been changed into flesh, bones, hair, and the whole body, and altered from its own nature? Or who ever heard in a Church, or even from Christians, that the Lord wore a body putatively [i.e., "seemingly", in other words: similar to Docetism], not in nature." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 2
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 2

quote: "Or who have been so venturesome as to say that Christ Who suffered in the flesh and was crucified is not Lord, Savior, God, and Son of the Father? Or how can they wish to be called Christians who say that the Word has descended upon a holy man as upon one of the prophets, and has not Himself become man, taking the body from Mary; but that Christ is one person, while the Word of God, Who before Mary and before the ages was Son of the Father, is another? Or how can they be Christians who say that the Son is one, and the Word of God another?" -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 2
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 59, Section 2

quote: "For what the heretical party of Eusebius and heirs of Arius have maintained and spread abroad, all the bishops who assembled have pronounced false and fictitious." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 47
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 47

quote: "Those who believe in Him ought not to be ungrateful for His many benefits." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 47
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 47

quote: "Formerly the character of the heretics was not evident. But now it is revealed and laid open to all. For the holy synod has taken cognisance of the calumnies these men have concocted against you [i.e., the Church in the Mareotis], and has had them in abhorrence, and has deposed Theodore, Valens, Ursacius, in Alexandria and the Mareotis by consent of all. The same notice has been given to other Churches also. And since the cruelty and tyranny practised by them against the Churches can no longer be borne, they have been cast out from the episcopate and expelled from the communion of all." -- Saint Athanasius the Great (died 373 AD), Personal Letters, Letter 46
reference: Personal Letters, Letter 46

quote: "Fold thyself around Him who is the very life itself, and live, O thou of men [i.e., speaking of Simeon at the temple] most venerable." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 7
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 7

quote: "What for God, who delights in man, is more magnificent than this merciful assumption of the manhood, illuminating with its resplendent rays those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death [Isaiah 42:7]?" -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 6
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 6

quote: "Him...who promised to show him [i.e., Simeon at the temple] His divine incarnation, as it were His hinder parts [Exodus 33:23]." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 6
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 6

quote: "Thou art our God, and Thee we adore; Thou art our holy Temple, and in Thee we pray; Thou art our Lawgiver, and Thee we obey; Thou art God of all things the First. Before Thee was no other god begotten of God the Father; neither after Thee shall there be any other son consubstantial and of one glory with the Father. And to know Thee is perfect righteousness, and to know Thy power is the root of immortality." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 6
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 6

quote: "[i.e., through the 'Sun of Righteoursness':] That hateful horror of darkness has been chased away; the power of the tyrant has been broken, death hath been destroyed, hell swallowed up, and all enmity dissolved before the face of peace; noxious diseases depart now that salvation looks forth; and the whole universe has been filled with the pure and clear light of truth. To which things Solomon alludes in the Book of Canticles, and begins thus: 'My beloved is mine, and I am his; he feedeth among the lilies until the day break, and the shadows flee away [Song of Solomon 2:16-17]'." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 5
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 5

quote: "The flame of the grace of my Lord does not consume, but illuminates thee." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 7
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 7

quote: "Receive the God who comes to thee, for He shall take away thine iniquities, and thoroughly purge thy sins." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 7
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 7

quote: "Put off that which is old, and clothe thyself with that which is new. For of these matters I think not that thou art ignorant." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 7
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 7

quote: "For out of Thy compassion for our low estate [i.e., the Fall of mankind] Thou hast shed forth upon us abundantly that goodness of Thine which is inexhaustible, and with Thy very nature cognate, having redeemed us by Thine only begotten Son, who is unchangeably like to Thee, and of one substance with Thee...But by means of that light, which is of one substance with Thee, Thou hast given light to those that sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, in order that in Thy light they might see the light of knowledge." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 8
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 8

quote: "It has seemed good to Thee...to fashion us again unto immortality; and Thou hast graciously given unto us a return to Paradise by means of Him who separated us from the joys of Paradise; and by means of Him who hath power to forgive sins Thou hast blotted out the handwriting which was against us [Colossians 2:14]." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 8
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 8

quote: "Not of works of righteousness which we have done, nor because we loved Thee...but...of Thine own...ineffable love toward the creature of Thine hands, hast confirmed Thy mercy toward us, and, pitying our estrangement from Thee, hast moved Thyself at the sight of our degradation to take us into compassion." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 8
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 8

quote: "For by the old man [i.e., Simeon] was represented the people of Israel, and the law now waxing old; whilst the widow [i.e., Anna] represents the Church of the Gentiles, which had been up to this point a widow." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 11
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 11

quote: "Her very name [i.e., Anna] also pre-signifies the Church, that by the grace of Christ and God is justified in baptism. For Anna is, by interpretation, grace." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 12
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 12

quote: "To us He condescended, that Word who was always with the Father co-existent God." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 13
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 13

quote: "Nor, again, did He come into the world to restore; nor will He restore, as has been imagined by some impious advocates of the devil [i.e., speaking of Origen and Origenism], those wicked demons who once fell from light." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 13
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 13

quote: "He was made man for ever [i.e., after the Incarnation], and without change [i.e., with His divinity], in order that by His fellowship with us, and our joining on to Him, the ingress of sin into us might be stopped, its strength being broken by degrees, and itself as wax being melted, by that fire which the Lord, when He came, sent upon the earth [Luke 12:49]." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 13
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 13

quote: "Simeon, thou earliest host of our holy religion, and teacher of the resurrection of the faithful, be our patron and advocate with that Saviour God, whom thou wast deemed worthy to receive into thine arms. We, together with thee, sing our praises to Christ." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 14
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 14

quote: "Wherefore, we pray thee, the most excellent among women, who boastest in the confidence of thy maternal honours, that thou wouldest unceasingly keep us in remembrance. O holy mother of God, remember us, I say, who make our boast in thee, and who in hymns august celebrate the memory, which will ever live, and never fade away." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 14
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 14

quote: "Hail to thee for ever, thou virgin mother of God, our unceasing joy, for unto thee do I again return." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 14
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 14

quote: "For the hymns which we offer to thee [i.e., speaking of the Theotokos (the Virgin Mary)], O thou most holy and admirable habitation of God, are no merely useless and ornamental words. Nor, again, is thy spiritual laudation mere secular trifling, or the shoutings of a false flattery, O thou who of God art praised; thou who to God gavest suck; who by nativity givest unto mortals their beginning of being, but they are of clear and evident truth. But the time would fail us, ages and succeeding generations too, to render unto thee thy fitting salutation as the mother of the King Eternal, even as somewhere the illustrious prophet says, 'teaching us how incomprehensible thou art [Baruch 3:24-25]'." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 10
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 10

quote: "Hail! hail! mother and handmaid of God [i.e., speaking of the Theotokos (the Virgin Mary)]. Hail! hail! thou to whom the great Creditor of all is a debtor. We are all debtors to God, but to thee He is Himself indebted." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 10
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 10

quote: "Mother of God [i.e., speaking of the Theotokos (the Virgin Mary)], thou that givest light to the faithful. Thou art the circumscription, so to speak, of Him who cannot be circumscribed; the root of the most beautiful flower; the mother of the Creator; the nurse of the Nourisher; the circumference of Him who embraces all things; the upholder of Him [Hebrews 1:3] who upholds all things by His word; the gate through which God appears in the flesh [Ezekiel 44:2]; the tongs of that cleansing coal [Isaiah 6:6]; the bosom in small of that bosom which is all-containing; the fleece of wool [Judges 6:37], the mystery of which cannot be solved; the well of Bethlehem, that reservoir of life which David longed for, out of which the draught of immortality gushed forth; the mercy-seat from which God in human form was made known unto men; the spotless robe of Him who clothes Himself with light as with a garment." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 10
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 10

quote: "The golden pot also, as a most certain type [i.e., types of the Theotokos (the Virgin Mary) in the Old Testament], preserved the manna contained in it, which in other cases was changed day by day, unchanged, and keeping fresh for ages." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 9
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 9

quote: "Then, again, that hard and rugged rock [Exodus 17:6], which imaged forth the grace and refreshment which has sprung out from thee [i.e., speaking of the Theotokos (the Virgin Mary)]...brought forth abundantly in the desert out of its thirsty sides a healing draught for the fainting people. Yea, moreover, the rod of the priest which, without culture, blossomed forth in fruit [Numbers 17:8]...furnished no contemptible symbol of thy supernatural child-bearing. What, moreover? Hath not the mighty Moses expressly declared, that on account of these types of thee, hard to be understood, he delayed longer on the mountain, in order that he might learn, O holy one, the mysteries that with thee are connected? For being commanded to build the ark as a sign and similitude of this thing...he appointed it to be the receptacle of the law, and covered it with the wings of the cherubim, most evidently pre-signifying thee, the mother of God, who hast conceived Him without corruption, and in an ineffable manner brought forth Him who is Himself, as it were, the very consistence of incorruption, and that within the limits of the five and a half circles of the world." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 9
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 9

quote: "That bush which could not be touched [Exodus 3:2], which beforehand shadowed forth thy figure [i.e., speaking of the Theotokos (the Virgin Mary)] endowed with divine majesty, bare God without being consumed, who manifested Himself to the prophet just so far as He willed to be seen." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 9
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 9

quote: "But what shall I say to thee, O mother-virgin and virgin-mother [i.e., speaking of the Theotokos (the Virgin Mary)]? For the praise even of her who is not man’s work exceeds the power of man. Wherefore the dimness of my poverty I will make bright with the splendour of the gifts of the spirits that around thee shine, and offering to thee of thine own, from the immortal meadows I will pluck a garland for thy sacred and divinely crowned head. With thine ancestral hymns will I greet thee, O daughter of David, and mother of the Lord and God of David. For it were both base and inauspicious to adorn thee, who in thine own glory excellest with that which belongeth unto another. Receive, therefore, O lady most benignant, gifts precious, and such as are fitted to thee alone, O thou who art exalted above all generations, and who, amongst all created things, both visible and invisible, shinest forth as the most honourable." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 9
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 9

quote: "For if to the ark, which was the image and type of thy [i.e., speaking of the Theotokos (the Virgin Mary)] sanctity...what sort of veneration is due to thee from us who are of creation the least, to thee who art indeed a queen; to thee, the living ark of God, the Lawgiver; to thee, the heaven that contains Him who can be contained of none? For since thou, O holy virgin, hast dawned as a bright day upon the world and hast brought forth the Sun of Righteousness." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 5
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 5

quote: "Tremendous, verily, is the mystery connected with thee, O virgin mother, thou spiritual throne, glorified and made worthy of God. Thou hast brought forth, before the eyes of those in heaven and earth, a pre-eminent wonder." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 5
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 5

quote: "She goes up, therefore to the temple, she who was more exalted than the temple, clothed with a double glory—the glory, I say, of undefiled virginity, and that of ineffable fecundity, the benediction of the law, and the sanctification of grace." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 4
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 4

quote: "The holy mother [i.e., the Theotokos (the Virgin Mary)] goes up to the temple to exhibit to the law a new and strange wonder, even that child long expected, who opened the virgin’s womb, and yet did not burst the barriers of virginity; that child, superior to the law, who yet fulfilled the law; that child that was at once before the law, and yet after it; that child, in short, who was of her incarnate beyond the law of nature. For in other cases every womb being first opened by connection with a man, and, being impregnated by his seed, receives the beginning of conception...But the womb of this virgin, without being opened before, or being impregnated with seed, gave birth to an offspring that transcended nature, while at the same time it was cognate to it, and that without detriment to the indivisible unity, so that the miracle was the more stupendous, the prerogative of virginity likewise remaining intact." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 4
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 4

quote: "She [i.e., the Theotokos (the Virgin Mary)] hath brought forth her first-born Son, even the only-begotten Son of God, Him, I say, who in the heavens above shone forth as the only-begotten, without mother, from out His Father’s substance, and preserved the virginity of His natural unity undivided and inseparable; and who on earth, in the virgin’s nuptial chamber, joined to Himself the nature of Adam, like a bridegroom, by an inalienable union, and preserved His mother’s purity uncorrupt and uninjured—Him, in short, who in heaven was begotten without corruption, and on earth brought forth in a manner quite unspeakable."-- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 3
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 3

quote: "It became indeed the Lord of the law and the prophets to do all things in accordance with His own law, and not to make void the law, but to fulfil it, and rather to connect with the fulfilment of the law the beginning of His grace...And He who makes us free from the law, became subject to the law; and there is offered for Him, who hath sanctified us, a pair of clean birds, in testimony of those who approach clean and blameless."-- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 3
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 3

quote: "The sacred Trinity, which now, by the appearance of God in the flesh, hath even lighted upon earth...For we believe that, together with the Son, who was made man for our sakes, according to the good pleasure of His will, was also present the Father, who is inseparable from Him as to His divine nature, anal also the Spirit, who is of one and the same essence with Him."-- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 2
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 2

quote: "God of His compassion toward us foreordained has come to pass, He hath given it fulfilment because of that love for man which is so becoming to Him."-- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 1
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 1

quote: "The Lord...sitting on a living and not inanimate ark [i.e., speaking of the Incarnation], as upon the mercy-seat, He comes forth in solemn procession upon the earth. The publican, when he touches this ark, comes away just; the harlot, when she approaches this, is remoulded, as it were, and becomes chaste; the leper, when he touches this, is restored whole without pain. It repulses none; it shrinks from none; it imparts the gifts of healing, without itself contracting any disease; for the Lord, who loves and cares for man, in it makes His resting-place."-- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 1
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 1

quote: "No longer does the stern decree of the law bear sway, but the grace of the Lord reigneth, drawing all men to itself by saving long-suffering."-- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 1
reference: Oration Concerning Simeon and Anna, Section 1

quote: "For martyrdom is so admirable and desirable, that the Lord, the Son of God Himself, honoring it, testified, 'He thought it not robbery to be equal with God [Philippians 2:5],' that He might honor man to whom He descended with this gift." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Fragments, From His Discourse Concerning Martyrs
reference: Fragments, From His Discourse Concerning Martyrs

quote: "In truth, our evil comes out of our want of resemblance to God, and our ignorance of Him; and, on the other hand, our great good consists in our resemblance to Him. And, therefore, our conversion and faith in the Being who is incorruptible and divine, seems to be truly our proper good, and ignorance and disregard of Him our evil; if, at least, those things which are produced in us and of us, being the evil effects of sin, are to be considered ours." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Fragments, From the Works of Methodius Against Porphyry, Fragment 3
reference: Fragments, From the Works of Methodius Against Porphyry, Fragment 3
tags: God is not the author of evil

quote: "Then repentance effaces every sin, when there is no delay after the fall of the soul, and the disease is not suffered to go on through a long interval. For then evil will not have power to leave its mark in us, when it is drawn up at the moment of its being set down like a plant newly planted." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Fragments, From the Works of Methodius Against Porphyry, Fragment 2
reference: Fragments, From the Works of Methodius Against Porphyry, Fragment 2

quote: "Origen, after having fabled many things concerning the eternity of the universe, adds this also: Nor yet from Adam, as some say, did man, previously not existing, first take his existence and come into the world. Nor again did the world begin to be made six days before the creation of Adam [i.e., Origen is presented here as teaching the pre-existence of beings before Adam and denying that creation simply began with the six days of Genesis.]...This is what Origen says seriously, and mark how he trifles." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Fragments, Extracts from the Work on Things Created, Section 9
reference: Fragments, Extracts from the Work on Things Created, Section 9

quote: "For Wisdom is said by one of the Divine band to speak in this manner concerning herself: 'The Lord created me the beginning of His ways for His works: of old He laid my foundation [Proverbs 8:22]'...Now consider whether the saying: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God [John 1:1-2];'—whether these statements be not in agreement with those. For we must say that the Beginning, out of which the most upright Word came forth, is the Father and Maker of all things, in whom it was. And the words, 'The same was in the beginning with God [John 1:2],' seem to indicate the position of authority of the Word, which He had with the Father before the world came into existence; 'beginning' signifying His power. And so, after the peculiar unbeginning beginning, who is the Father, He is the beginning of other things, by whom all things are made." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Fragments, Extracts from the Work on Things Created, Section 8
reference: Fragments, Extracts from the Work on Things Created, Section 8

quote: "Let us suppose a beautiful statue standing upon its base; and that those who behold it...differ among themselves, some trying to make out that it had been made, others that it had not...If...the statue is declared to be by itself perfect and not made, and to have no need of art [i.e., of an artist], then we must allow, in accordance with that pernicious heresy, that it is self-made...For if this statue has need of nothing, and has no beginning of existence, for this reason, according to you, a maker never made it...Now we must compare the artificer to God, and the statue to the world. But how then, O foolish men, can you imagine the creation to be co-eternal with its Artificer, and to have no need of an artificer [i.e., Saint Methodius critiquing Origenism]?" -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Fragments, Extracts from the Work on Things Created, Section 5
reference: Fragments, Extracts from the Work on Things Created, Section 5

quote: "Origen says that what he calls the Centaur is the universe which is co-eternal with the only wise and independent God [i.e., this wording is misleading as it seems to suggest Origen "calls the Centaur the universe", but a better wording is: "Origen, who he (Saint Methodius) calls the Centaur..." This becomes more clear in Section 4; however, more can be found here: https://www.ccel.org/ccel/wace/biodict.html?term=methodius#:~:text=centaur]. For he says, since there is no workman without some work, or maker without something made, so neither is there an Almighty without an object of His power...It is impossible, therefore, to say that the universe is not unbeginning and co-eternal with God. To whom the saint replies [i.e., Saint Methodius or another Saint critiquing the errors of Origenism], in the person of another, asking, 'Do you not consider God the beginning and fountain of wisdom and glory, and in short of all virtue in substance and not by acquisition?'" -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Fragments, Extracts from the Work on Things Created, Section 2
reference: Fragments, Extracts from the Work on Things Created, Section 2

quote: "Nor are we to understand the words, 'Cast not your pearls before swine [Matthew 7:6],' as forbidding us to cast before the impious and unbelieving the deep and sanctifying doctrines of faith in Christ; but we must take the pearls to mean virtues, with which the soul is adorned as with precious pearls; and not to cast them before swine, as meaning that we are not to cast these virtues, such as chastity, temperance, righteousness, and truth, that we are not to cast these to impure pleasures, for these are like swine, lest they, fleeing from the virtues, cause the soul to live a swinish and a vicious life." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Fragments, Extracts from the Work on Things Created, Section 1
reference: Fragments, Extracts from the Work on Things Created, Section 1

quote: "Whence also the Word descended into our world, and was incarnate of our body, in order that, having fashioned it to a more divine image, He might raise it incorrupt, although it had been dissolved by time." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Fragments, On the History of Jonah, From the Book on the Resurrection, Section 2
reference: Fragments, On the History of Jonah, From the Book on the Resurrection, Section 2

quote: "For consider that God had images of Himself made as of gold, that is of a purer spiritual substance, as the angels; and others of clay or brass, as ourselves. He united the soul which was made in the image of God to that which was earthy. As, then, we must here honour all the images of a king, on account of the form which is in them, so also it is incredible that we who are the images of God should be altogether destroyed as being without honour." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Fragments, On the History of Jonah, From the Book on the Resurrection, Section 2
reference: Fragments, On the History of Jonah, From the Book on the Resurrection, Section 2

topic: On the Life of the World to Come
quote: "For in that age [i.e., the age to come; after our departure of this present life] there is neither past nor future, but only the present." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Fragments, On the History of Jonah, From the Book on the Resurrection, Section 2
reference: Fragments, On the History of Jonah, From the Book on the Resurrection, Section 2

quote: "As, then, Jonah spent three days and as many nights in the whale’s belly, and was delivered up sound again, so shall we all, who have passed through the three stages of our present life on earth—I mean the beginning, the middle, and the end, of which all this present time consists—rise again." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Fragments, On the History of Jonah, From the Book on the Resurrection, Section 2
reference: On the History of Jonah, From the Book on the Resurrection, Section 2

quote: "The history of Jonah contains a great mystery. For it seems that the whale signifies Time, which never stands still, but is always going on, and consumes the things which are made by long and shorter intervals. But Jonah, who fled from the presence of God, is himself the first man who, having transgressed the law...And the ship in which he embarked...is this brief and hard life in the present time...And the storm and the tempests which beat against us are the temptations of this life...And the casting of Jonah from the ship into the sea, signifies the fall of the first man from life to death...And his being swallowed by the whale signifies our inevitable removal by time. For the belly in which Jonah, when he was swallowed, was concealed, is the all-receiving earth, which receives all things which are consumed by time." -- Saint Methodius of Olympus (died 311 AD), Fragments, On the History of Jonah, From the Book on the Resurrection, Section 1
reference: Fragments, On the History of Jonah, From the Book on the Resurrection, Section 1

quote: "For when we say simply one subsistence of God the Word, we do not err. In like manner, also, Leontius the Byzantine considered this phrase to refer to nature, and not to subsistence. But in the Defence which he wrote in reply to the attacks that Theodoret made on the second anathema, the blessed Cyril says this: 'The nature of the Word, that is, the subsistence, which is the Word itself.' So that ‘the nature of the Word’ means neither the subsistence alone, nor 'the common nature of the subsistence,' but 'the common nature viewed as a whole in the subsistence of the Word.'" -- Saint John of Damascus (676-749 AD), An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 3, Chapter 11
reference: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 3, Chapter 11

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "Musical instruments, those which are loud and harsh are the most unpleasant to the ear, such as the drum and trumpet; whereas those which are not so, but are soothing, these are pleasant, as the flute and lyre and pipe. Let us then prepare our soul so as never to cry aloud, and thus shall we be enabled also to gain the mastery over our anger. And when we have cut out this, we ourselves shall be the first to enjoy the calm, and we shall sail into that peaceful haven, which God grant we may all attain." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 15 (Ephesians 4:31)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 15 (Ephesians 4:31)

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "Observe the progress of mischief. Bitterness produces wrath, wrath anger, anger clamor, clamor railing, that is, revilings; next from evil-speaking it goes on to blows, from blows to wounds, from wounds to death." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 15 (Ephesians 4:31)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 15 (Ephesians 4:31)

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "Cut off clamor, and you will clip the wings of anger...Bind the hands of the boxer, and then bid him strike. He will be unable to do so. So likewise will wrath be disarmed. But clamor raises it, even where it does not exist." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 15 (Ephesians 4:31)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 15 (Ephesians 4:31)

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "Clamor carries anger, as a horse his rider; trip the horse, and you will throw the rider." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 15 (Ephesians 4:31)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 15 (Ephesians 4:31)

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "For it is not possible for a soul like this [i.e., an angry/wrathful person] to be in tranquillity, but the very root of 'anger' and 'wrath' is bitterness. The man of this character is both sullen, and never unbends his soul; he is always moody, always gloomy." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 15 (Ephesians 4:31)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 15 (Ephesians 4:31)

quote: "What is 'corrupt speech [Ephesians 4:29]'? That which is said elsewhere to be also 'idle, backbiting, filthy communication, jesting, foolish talking [Ephesians 5:4]'...And well too does he give advice concerning conversation; inasmuch as we shall pay the penalty, not for our deeds only, but also for our words. 'But such as is good,' he proceeds, 'for edifying, as the need may be, that it may give grace to them that hear [Ephesians 4:29]'. That is to say, What edifies your neighbor, that only speak, not a word more. For to this end God gave you a mouth and a tongue, that you might give thanks to Him, that you might build up your neighbor. So that if you destroy that building, better were it to be silent, and never to speak at all." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 14 (Ephesians 4:29)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 14 (Ephesians 4:29)

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "And how then shall you be able to say with them [i.e., the Seraphim], 'Holy, Holy, Holy [Isaiah 6:1-3]', if you use your mouth for reviling? Tell me, I pray. Suppose there were a royal vessel, and that always full of royal dainties, and set apart for that purpose, and then that any one of the servants were to take and use it for holding dung. Would he ever venture again, after it had been filled with dung, to store it away with those other vessels, set apart for those other uses? Surely not. Now railing is like this, reviling is like this." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 14 (Ephesians 4:30)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 14 (Ephesians 4:30)

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "Be at enmity, but be so with the devil, and not with a member of your own. For this purpose it is that God has armed us with anger, not that we should thrust the sword against our own bodies, but that we should baptize the whole blade in the devil's breast. There bury the sword up to the hilt." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 14 (Ephesians 4:25-27)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 14 (Ephesians 4:25-27)

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "How shall we extinguish the flame [i.e., of anger]? By reflecting on our own sins, and how much we have to answer for to God; by reflecting that we are wreaking vengeance, not on an enemy, but on ourselves; by reflecting that we are delighting the devil, that we are strengthening our enemy, our real enemy, and that for him we are doing wrong to our own members." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 14 (Ephesians 4:25-27)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 14 (Ephesians 4:25-27)

quote: "But when he [i.e., the devil] causes us to relax a little, he rushes in like a torrent." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 14 (Ephesians 4:25-27)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 14 (Ephesians 4:25-27)

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "For observe, when anger is excited above what is meet, then it rushes out into insult, then it commits every sort of injury; so does inordinate passion for beauty, for riches, for glory, or for anything else." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:24)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:24)

quote: "Enjoy your baths, take care of your body, and throw yourself freely into the world, and keep a household, have your servants to wait on you, and make free use of your meats and drinks [i.e., Saint John was just speaking of Monastics and how not everyone can tolerate that way of life]! But everywhere drive out excess, for that it is which causes sin, and the same thing, whatever it be, if it becomes excessive, becomes a sin; so that excess is nothing else than sin." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:24)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:24)

quote: "Do you not see them that are in the mountains? They forsake both houses, and wives, and children, and all preeminence, and shut themselves away from the world, and clothe themselves in sackcloth, and strew ashes beneath them; they wear collars hung about their necks, and have pent themselves up in a narrow cell. Nor do they stop here, but torture themselves with fastings and continual hunger. Did I now enjoin you to do the like, would ye not all start away? Would ye not say, it is intolerable? But no, I say not that we must needs do anything like this:—I would fain indeed that it were so, still I lay down no law." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:24)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:24)

quote: "Virtue is not toilsome, she is not difficult to attain." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:24)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:24)

quote: "Let us strip ourselves of our riches, that we be not stripped of righteousness. The garb of wealth mars this garment [i.e., the garment of righteousness]. It is a robe of thorns...Lasciviousness strips us of this garment; for it is a fire, and the fire will consume this garment. Wealth is a moth; and as the moth eats through all things alike, and spares not even silken garments, so does this also. All these therefore let us put off, that we may become righteous, that we may 'put on the new man [Ephesians 4:24]'." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:24)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:24)

quote: "Our part then is, never to put off the garment of righteousness, which also the Prophet calls, 'the garment of salvation [Isaiah 61:10]', that so we may be made like God. For He indeed has put on righteousness. This garment let us put on. Now the word, 'put on', plainly declares nothing else, than that we should never at all put it off...So then it is not for one day, nor for two, nor for three, but he would have us ever arrayed in virtue, and never stripped of this garment. For a man is not so disfigured when he is stripped of his clothing, as when he is stripped of his virtue." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:24)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:24)

quote: "How does he say to them who are already clothed, 'put on [Ephesians 4:24]'? He is now speaking of that clothing which is from life and good works. Before, the clothing was from Baptism, whereas now it is from the daily life and from works." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:24)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:24)

quote: "For man is created henceforth, not of water, nor of earth, but 'in righteousness and holiness of truth [Ephesians 4:24]'. What is this? He straightway created him, he means, to be a son: for this takes place from Baptism." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:24)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:24)

quote: "Now as to undress one's self and to dress one's self is easy, so may we see it is with virtue and vice. The young man is strong; wherefore let us also become strong for the performance of good actions. The young man has no wrinkle, therefore neither should we have. The young man wavers not, nor is he easily taken with diseases, therefore neither should we be." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:24)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:24)

quote: "That is to say [i.e., commenting on Ephesians 4:21-22], it was not on these terms that you entered into covenant. What is found among us is not vanity, but truth. As the doctrines are true, so is the life also. Sin is vanity and falsehood; but a right life is truth." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:22)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:22)

quote: "'Who being past feeling', says he, 'gave themselves up to lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness; but you did not so learn Christ [Ephesians 4:19-20]'. Here he shows us, that the cause of their hardening was their way of life, and that their life was the consequence of their own indolence and want of feeling." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:17-19)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 13 (Ephesians 4:17-19)

quote: "You may see a man washing himself from the pollution of a dead body, but from dead works, never." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 12 (Ephesians 4:17)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 12 (Ephesians 4:17)

quote: "Riches are vain when they are spent upon luxury; but they cease to be vain when they are 'dispersed and given to the needy [Psalm 112:9]'." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 12 (Ephesians 4:17)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 12 (Ephesians 4:17)

quote: "What is vanity of mind? It is the being busied about vain things. And what are those vain things, but all things in the present life?" -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 12 (Ephesians 4:17)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 12 (Ephesians 4:17)

quote: "I speak not of you that are present, but of those who are deserting from us [i.e., in schism, heresy, and in causing division in the Church]. The act is adultery." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 11 (Ephesians 4:15-16)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 11 (Ephesians 4:15-16)

quote: "'Children', says he, 'tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind [Ephesians 4:14]'. Tell me, do you think this is enough, to say that they are orthodox? Is then the ordination of clergy past and done away? And what is the advantage of other things, if this be not strictly observed? For as we must needs contend for the faith; so must we for this also. For if it is lawful for any one, according to the phrase of them of old, 'to fill his hands', and to become a priest, let all approach to minister [i.e., there must be proper ordination of those in the priesthood]. In vain has this altar been raised, in vain the fullness of the Church, in vain the number of the priests. Let us take them away and destroy them. God forbid! you will say. You are doing these things, and do ye say, God forbid? How say ye, God forbid, when the very things are taking place [i.e., there were many causing divisions in schisms within the Church]? I speak and testify, not looking to my own interest, but to your salvation." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 11 (Ephesians 4:15-16)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 11 (Ephesians 4:15-16)

quote: "I mean these remarks [i.e., warnings of schism and division in the Church] for those who give themselves up indiscriminately to the men who are dividing the Church. For if on the one hand those men have doctrines also contrary to ours, then on that account further it is not right to mix with them: if, on the other hand, they hold the same opinions, the reason for not mixing with them is greater still. And why so? Because then the disease is from lust of authority. Do you not know what was the fate of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram [Numbers 16:1-35]?...Shall it be said, 'Their faith is the same, they are orthodox as well as we'? If so, why then are they not with us? There is 'one Lord, one faith, one baptism [Ephesians 4:5]'. If their cause is right, then is ours wrong; if ours is right, then is theirs wrong." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 11 (Ephesians 4:15-16)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 11 (Ephesians 4:15-16)

quote: "Now a certain holy man said what might seem to be a bold thing; yet, nevertheless, he spoke it out. What then is this? He said, that not even the blood of martyrdom can wash out this sin [i.e., the sin of causing division in the Church]. For tell me for what do you suffer as a martyr? Is it not for the glory of Christ? Thou then that yieldest up your life for Christ's sake, how do you lay waste the Church, for whose sake Christ yielded up His life?" -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 11 (Ephesians 4:15-16)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 11 (Ephesians 4:15-16)

quote: "Nothing so provokes God's anger as the division of the Church. Yea, though we have achieved ten thousand glorious acts, yet shall we, if we cut to pieces the fullness of the Church, suffer punishment no less sore than they who mangled His body." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 11 (Ephesians 4:15-16)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 11 (Ephesians 4:15-16)

quote: "For there are two kinds of separation from the body of the Church; the one, when we wax cold in love, the other, when we dare commit things unworthy of our belonging to that body; for in either way we cut ourselves off from the 'fullness of Christ [Colossians 2:9-10]'." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 11 (Ephesians 4:15-16)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 11 (Ephesians 4:15-16)

quote: "Hence he says, there is 'one body [Ephesians 4:4]'; one, both by sympathy, and by not opposing the good of others, and by sharing their joy, having expressed all at once by this figure. He then beautifully adds, 'and one Spirit', showing that from the one body there will be one Spirit: or, that it is possible that there may be indeed one body, and yet not one Spirit; as, for instance, if any member of it should be a friend of heretics [i.e., the Body will not be in division and unagreed on doctrine]: or else he is, by this expression, shaming them into unanimity, saying, as it were, 'You who have received one Spirit, and have been made to drink at one fountain, ought not to be divided in mind [1 Corinthians 12:13]'; or else by spirit here he means their zeal." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 11 (Ephesians 4:4-7)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 11 (Ephesians 4:4-7)

quote: "The body is not disjoined from the spirit, for then would it not be a body. Thus it is customary also with us, touching things which are united, and which have any great consistency or coherence, to say, they are one body. And thus again, touching union, we take that to be a body which is under one head. If there be one head, then is there one body. The body is composed of members both honorable and dishonorable...Now why am I saying this? There are great numbers in the Church; there are those who, like the head, are raised up to a height; who, like the eyes that are in the head, survey heavenly things, who stand far aloof from the earth, and have nothing in common with it, while others occupy the rank of feet, and tread upon the earth; of healthy feet indeed, for to tread upon the earth is no crime in feet, but to run to evil." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 10 (Ephesians 4:5)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 10 (Ephesians 4:5)

quote: "And the prophets too would not have written of One, of whom they knew not what they said; whereas they both knew Him, and worshipped Him. Thus then were they also 'one body'." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 10 (Ephesians 4:5)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 10 (Ephesians 4:5)
tags: Old Testament Saints believed in Christ

quote: "Now what is this one body [i.e., Ephesians 4:4]? The faithful throughout the whole world, both which are, and which have been, and which shall be. And again, they that before Christ's coming pleased God, are one body. How so? Because they also knew Christ. Whence does this appear? 'Your father Abraham', says He, 'rejoiced to see My day, and he saw it, and was glad' [John 8:56]." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 10 (Ephesians 4:5)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 10 (Ephesians 4:5)
tags: Old Testament Saints believed in Christ

topic: On Faith and Hope and Love
quote: "Let us give thanks to God, and follow after every virtue; and before all things, let us with all strictness practice love, that we may be counted worthy to attain the promised blessings." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 9 (Ephesians 4:1-3)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 9 (Ephesians 4:1-3)

quote: "It was the love of God that seated man upon the kingly throne. It was the love of God that manifested God upon earth. It was the love of God that made the Lord a servant. It was the love of God that caused the Beloved to be delivered up for His enemies, the Son for them that hated Him, the Lord for His servants, God for men, the free for slaves." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 9 (Ephesians 4:1-3)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 9 (Ephesians 4:1-3)

topic: On Faith and Hope and Love
quote: "He who knows not how to love, will therefore commit many evil actions; and he who commits evil actions, knows not what it is to love." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 9 (Ephesians 4:1-3)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 9 (Ephesians 4:1-3)

topic: On Faith and Hope and Love
quote: "If you, he [i.e. the Apostle Paul in Ephesians 4:2] would say, are not forbearing to your neighbor, how shall God be forbearing to you? If you bear not with your fellow-servant, how shall the Master bear with you? Wherever there is love, all things are to be borne." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 9 (Ephesians 4:1-3)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 9 (Ephesians 4:1-3)

topic: On Temptations and Sin and the Passions
quote: "For it is possible for a man to be lowly, and yet quick and irritable, and thus all is to no purpose; for oftentimes he will be possessed by his anger, and ruin all." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 9 (Ephesians 4:1-3)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 9 (Ephesians 4:1-3)

quote: "But how is it possible to 'walk worthily of it' [Ephesians 4:1]? 'With all lowliness [Ephesians 4:2]'. Such an one walks worthily. This is the basis of all virtue." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 9 (Ephesians 4:1-3)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 9 (Ephesians 4:1-3)

topic: On Faith and Hope and Love
quote: "Thus is it we ought to love our enemies, thus to imitate Christ...This is to love God, Who has enjoined it, Who has given it as His law. To imitate Him is to love our enemy. Consider it is not your enemy you are benefiting, but yourself; you are not loving him, but art obeying God. Knowing therefore these things, let us confirm our love one to another, that we may perform this duty perfectly, and attain those good things that are promised in Christ Jesus our Lord." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 7 (Ephesians 3:21)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 7 (Ephesians 3:21)

quote: "'The glory in the Church [Ephesians 3:21]'. Well might he say this, forasmuch as the Church alone can last on to eternity." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 7 (Ephesians 3:21)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 7 (Ephesians 3:21)

quote: "The Holy Spirit speaks in the sacred Scriptures, and says, 'By almsgiving and faith sins are purged [Proverbs 16:6].' Not assuredly those sins which had been previously contracted [i.e., before our baptism], for those are purged by the blood and sanctification of Christ. Moreover, He says again, 'As water extinguisheth fire, so almsgiving quencheth sin [Sirach 3:30].' Here also it is shown and proved, that as in the laver of saving water [i.e., baptism] the fire of Gehenna is extinguished, so by almsgiving and works of righteousness the flame of sins is subdued. And because in baptism remission of sins is granted once for all, constant and ceaseless labor, following the likeness of baptism, once again bestows the mercy of God." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Treatises, Treatise 8, Section 2
reference: Treatises, Treatise 8, Section 2

quote: "By almsgiving we may wash away whatever foulness we subsequently contract." -- Saint Cyprian of Carthage (200-258 AD), Treatises, Treatise 8, Section 1
reference: Treatises, Treatise 8, Section 1

quote: "'Because through Him we both have our access in one Spirit unto the Father [Ephesians 2:18]', not ye [i.e., Gentiles] less, and they [i.e., Jews] more, but all by one and the same grace. The wrath He appeased by His death, and has made us meet for the Father's love through the Spirit [i.e., Christ brought peace (the preceding sentence to this quote) by breaking down the ‘middle wall’ as Saint John mentions on Ephesians 2:14, he is not advocating for Penal Substitutionary Atonement]." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 6 (Ephesians 2:17-22)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 6 (Ephesians 2:17-22)

quote: "So the eyes are good, but without light, will commit innumerable errors; this, however, is the fault of their weakness, not of nature. Were the errors natural, then should we never be able to use them aright at all. For nothing that is natural is evil." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 5 (Ephesians 2:16)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 5 (Ephesians 2:16)
tags: God is not the author of evil

quote: "Some indeed affirm that he means the wall of the Jews against the Greeks [i.e., referencing 'the middle wall of separation' in Ephesians 2:14], because it did not allow the Jews to hold intercourse with the Greeks. To me, however, this does not seem to be the meaning, but rather that he calls the enmity in the flesh, a middle wall, in that it is a common barrier, cutting us off alike from God. As the Prophet says, 'Your iniquities separate between you and Me [Isaiah 59:2]'; for that enmity which He had both against Jews and Gentiles was, as it were, a middle wall." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 5 (Ephesians 2:13-15)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 5 (Ephesians 2:13-15)

quote: "His death, says the Apostle, has 'slain' the enmity. He has 'wounded' and 'killed' it...He does not say 'having dissolved', he does say 'having cancelled [i.e., such as in Colossians 2:14]', but what is stronger than all, 'having slain', so that it never should rise again. How then is it that it does rise again? From our exceeding depravity. For as long as we abide in the body of Christ, as long as we are united, it rises not again, but lies dead." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 5 (Ephesians 2:16)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 5 (Ephesians 2:16)

topic: On Faith and Hope and Love
quote: "For he makes a wide distinction between 'commandments' and 'ordinances' [i.e., in Ephesians 2:15]. He either then means 'faith', calling that an 'ordinance', (for by faith alone He saved us,) or he means 'precept', such as Christ gave, when He said, 'But I say unto you, that you are not to be angry at all [Matthew 5:22]'. That is to say, 'If you shall believe that God raised Him from the dead, you shall be saved [Romans 10:6-9]'...Instead of a certain manner of life, He brought in faith [i.e., instead of the Mosaic Law, rituals, food laws, circumcision, etc.]. For that He might not save us to no purpose, He both Himself underwent the penalty [i.e., of death], and also required of men the faith that is by doctrines." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 5 (Ephesians 2:13-15)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 5 (Ephesians 2:13-15)

quote: "For he says, 'Having abolished the law of commandments contained in ordinances [Ephesians 2:15]'. Oh! amazing loving-kindness! He gave us a law that we should keep it, and when we kept it not, and ought to have been punished, He even abrogated the law itself." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 5 (Ephesians 2:13-15)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 5 (Ephesians 2:13-15)

quote: "The promise indeed He gave to the Israelites, but they were unworthy; to us He gave no promise, nay, we were even strangers, we had nothing in common with them; yet has He made us one, not by knitting us to them, but by knitting both them and us together into one." -- Saint John Chrysostom (347-407 AD), Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 5 (Ephesians 2:13-15)
reference: Homilies on Ephesians, Homily 5 (Ephesians 2:13-15)

quote: "So Paul, the imitator of Christ, says, 'being made conformable unto his death; if by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead [Philippians 3:10-11].' How then are we made in the likeness of His death? In that we were buried with Him by baptism. What then is the manner of the burial?
